newsitem.title: USA: Expansion team Super Bowl not much fun for advertisers.
newsitem.headline: Expansion team Super Bowl not much fun for advertisers.

text.p: The Super Bowl will be the year's top-rated television show, no doubt, but with expansion and small-market teams vying for the game, sponsors who paid $1.3 million for 30 second commercials are jittery.

The big-time football franchises in Dallas, San Francisco and other major cities have already fallen by the wayside. Left in the running are Jacksonville, Fla., the No. 55 media market, Charlotte, No. 28, and Green Bay, No. 71.
Only the New England Patriots play in a top 10 market, in suburban Boston (No. 6).
All four teams play this Sunday, and two will advance to the Super Bowl on Jan. 26.
"I'm concerned about a Jacksonville-Carolina matchup," said Steve Grubbs, national media director for ad agency BBDO. "That could lead to a loss of 10 percent of the audience."
Grey Advertising media buyer Jon Mandel agreed. "It may be a concern. The expansion teams have not been around long enough to build up much of a national following."

For the advertisers, who booked their $1.3-million 30-second spots last year before the commercial time sold out, such a matchup seemed highly unlikely. The oddsmakers considered the chances one in 100,000 at the start of the season.

The National Pork Producers Council is one of a handful of advertisers that puts virtually all of its annual advertising budget into the Super Bowl. "I'm not worried," said Barry Pfouts, vice president/marketing for the group. "People will tune in at least for a while, even if it doesn't have the same built-in appeal fan support that Dallas or Chicago might bring."
But if he had to pick, Pfouts would prefer that the Green Bay Packers make it into the final round. The media buyers agreed.

"Green Bay has a unique history," said BBDO's Grubbs. "It has Brett Favre, arguably the best player in football, and Reggie White. Even though it's from a small market, Green Bay is a draw. It's important from a ratings standpoint that they be there."

Las Vegas oddsmakers say that's likely to happen, with Green Bay as the prohibitive favourite, a 3-1 pick to win its game this week against Carolina and go on to win as the National Football Conference representative in the Super Bowl.
But even the worst-case scenario isn't so bad for advertisers, said the media buyers.
"It's still going to be the top rated show of the year, regardless of who plays," said Grubbs. "It's like the Academy Awards. People just tune in every year."

Media consultant Erwin Ephron, of Ephron Papazian Ephron, said that "Along with the Olympics, it's one of the few remaining events where you can talk to the nation simultaneously. More importantly, they've managed to make it into an exhibition for advertisers, where people actually watch and critique the ads. It's a very interesting media phenomenon."

The game has become "the event" for not just football, but also for advertising, Ephron said. While the leading TV networks continue to lose market share the rest of the year, demand has remained strong for the Super Bowl, with advertisers booking all 50-odd available spots in advance -- at an average cost of $1.3 million a spot.
"For advertisers, it's the biggest stage in the world," said Bozell Worldwide/Chicago creative director David Wojdyla.
